```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

`dv_build_html()` writes a single HTML file with one page per predator,
modeled on the diet dashboard built for the southern Gulf of St. Lawrence. The
landing page shows one card per predator, with its stomach count and, if you
give a length column, its length range. Each predator page shows the diet in
up to three bands: distinct prey items, prey records (% of all records) and
weight (% of total weight). Every band has the same layout: one sunburst for
all the predator's records, one row of sunbursts per covariate you choose, and,
if you ask for them, crossed rows.

The data are the public ICES stomach-content extract that ships with the
package (ICES Stomach Content Database, ICES, Copenhagen; extract distributed
with the R package stomachr, Lindmark 2026; see `?ices_diet`). The preparation
chunks run; the chunks that write HTML files are shown but not run, because a
dashboard of this size takes a while to build.

## Preparing the data

The set-up is the one used in every vignette, restricted here to the four
predators with the most records, so that each page has enough stomachs per
panel:

```{r prep}
library(DietView)

# drop non-food items and nematodes (mostly parasites, not prey)
phylum <- ices_lineage$phylum[match(ices_diet$prey_aphia_id, ices_lineage$prey_aphia_id)]
dat <- ices_diet[ices_diet$item_type != "non_food" & !phylum %in% "Nematoda", ]

top <- c("Atlantic cod", "Whiting", "European plaice", "Atlantic mackerel")
dat <- dat[dat$predator_common %in% top, ]
```

### Length classes, predator by predator

Diets change with predator size, so length is the first stratum most people
want. One set of length classes does not fit four predators of different
sizes: a 25 cm mackerel is a small fish, a 25 cm cod a young one.
`dv_size_bins()` cuts lengths with breaks you choose, so give each predator its
own:

```{r lengths}
tapply(dat$length_cm, dat$predator_common, range)

breaks <- list(
  "Atlantic cod"      = c(0, 20, 30, 40, 50, 110),
  "Whiting"           = c(0, 20, 25, 30, 45),
  "European plaice"   = c(0, 20, 25, 30, 55),
  "Atlantic mackerel" = c(0, 25, 30, 35, 50)
)
dat$length_class <- NA_character_
for (p in names(breaks)) {
  i <- dat$predator_common == p
  dat$length_class[i] <- as.character(dv_size_bins(dat$length_cm[i], breaks[[p]]))
}
```

Check the number of stomachs per class before you build anything; a sunburst
from a handful of stomachs is not worth drawing:

```{r length-n}
stom <- unique(dat[, c("stomach_id", "predator_common", "length_class",
                       "region", "quarter")])
lapply(split(stom$length_class, stom$predator_common), table)
```

The breaks above were chosen so that every class holds at least a hundred
stomachs. Move them, or merge classes, where your data are thinner.

### Region and quarter

The other two strata are region and quarter. They are not balanced:

```{r strata-n}
table(stom$predator_common, stom$region)
table(stom$predator_common, stom$quarter)
```

```{r strata-values, include = FALSE}
mq <- table(stom$quarter[stom$predator_common == "Atlantic mackerel"])
mq <- mq[mq > 0]
pq <- table(stom$quarter[stom$predator_common == "European plaice"])
pq <- names(pq[pq > 0])
```

Mackerel were sampled in quarter `r names(mq)` only and never in the Baltic
Sea; plaice in quarters `r paste(pq, collapse = " and ")`. The dashboard omits
empty strata, so the mackerel page simply has one quarter panel. On the global
page, which pools the four predators, a comparison across quarters or regions
is also a comparison of whichever predators were sampled there, and with these
data of the countries that sampled them. The same goes for length: the global
page puts every predator's class with the same label in one panel (`[0, 20)`
holds small cod, plaice and whiting), so read length on the predator pages.

```{r spec}
spec <- dv_spec(
  predator       = "predator_common",
  predator_latin = "predator_latin",
  stomach        = "stomach_id",
  prey_id        = "prey_aphia_id",
  prey_name      = "prey_name",
  weight         = "prey_weight_g",
  count          = "prey_count",
  digestion      = "digestion_label",
  covariates     = c("region", "quarter", "length_class")
)
prep <- dv_prepare(dat, spec, taxonomy = "table", lineage = ices_lineage,
                   verbose = FALSE)
prep
```

## The simplest dashboard

Name the output file yourself. By default the build stays offline, so the
cards have no photo:

```{r simple, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet_dashboard.html"))
```

## Stratifying each band by covariates

`strata` picks the covariates that get their own row of sunbursts in every
band. `cross` adds crossed rows: `cross = list(c(inner, outer))` gives one row
per level of `outer`, with one sunburst per level of `inner` in that row.

```{r strata, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(
  prep,
  output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet_dashboard.html"),
  strata = c("region", "quarter", "length_class"),
  cross  = list(c("length_class", "region")),   # length classes within regions
  bands  = c("count", "occurrence", "weight"),
  length_col = "length_cm"
)
```

In `bands`, `"count"` is the distinct prey items band, `"occurrence"` the prey
records band and `"weight"` the weight band. Crossing multiplies the number of
panels: five cod length classes in three regions give up to fifteen sunbursts
per band, and some of them rest on few stomachs (see `stom` above). Each panel
prints its stomach count; read it before the sunburst. With these four
predators and this crossing, the file holds several hundred sunbursts: it took
about a minute to build and weighs about 20 MB. Drop a band or the crossing for
a lighter file.

To show individuals (%N) rather than records in the second band, add
`currency = "numbers"`. Records without a count, which here include almost all
the unidentified material, then contribute nothing to that band.

## Identification cards

Each predator card can show a photo and a short description. DietView looks for
a photo in this order: a local file you name in `species_info`, a local file in
`image_dir` named after the predator or its Latin name, then, if you ask for it,
an openly licensed photo from iNaturalist (`photo_source = "inaturalist"`) or
from Wikipedia and Wikimedia Commons (`photo_source = "wikipedia"`). The photo
is embedded in the HTML file, so the file stays complete on its own. To control
what is shown, supply your own description and photo:

```{r cards, eval = FALSE}
info <- list(
  "Atlantic cod" = list(
    desc  = "Demersal gadid; feeds on crustaceans and fish.",
    photo = "images/atlantic_cod.jpg"
  )
)
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet_dashboard.html"),
              species_info = info, image_dir = "images")
```

To fill the cards from iNaturalist, the predators' Latin names must be in the
spec; `ices_diet` has them in `predator_latin` (for example *Gadus morhua*,
*Merlangius merlangus*). Then ask for that source:

```{r cards-inat, eval = FALSE}
dv_build_html(prep, output = file.path(tempdir(), "diet_dashboard.html"),
              strata = c("region", "quarter", "length_class"),
              length_col = "length_cm",
              photo_source = "inaturalist",
              image_dir = file.path(tempdir(), "dietview-images"))
```

This needs an internet connection. Only photos under CC0, CC BY or CC BY-SA are
used unless you widen `licenses`, and each card shows the photographer and the
license, linked to the photo's page on iNaturalist. Keep those credits: they
are the condition under which the photos may be reused. Check the credit line
on each card before you share the file. The article on species cards gives the
details.

## Deploying to a folder

`dv_deploy()` calls `dv_build_html()` and writes the file into a folder of your
choice, for example one served by your web platform. It returns the path.

```{r deploy, eval = FALSE}
dv_deploy(prep, file = "dietview_dashboard.html",
          dir = file.path(tempdir(), "outputs"),
          strata = c("region", "quarter", "length_class"),
          cross  = list(c("length_class", "region")),
          length_col = "length_cm")
```

The dashboard is a snapshot. It holds the data as they were when you built it,
opens in any browser and needs neither R nor an internet connection. Say on the
page, or next to it, where the data come from: here "ICES Stomach Content
Database, ICES, Copenhagen".
